Arizona enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 32-2 overall and 16-2 in the Big 12, after winning both the Big 12 regular-season title and the conference tournament. ESPN’s team page lists the Wildcats at 32-2 and first in the Big 12, while Arizona’s official cumulative stats show 34 games played entering the NCAA field. The profile is that of a power team first and a finesse team second: 86.1 points per game, 50.2% from the field, 42.5 rebounds per game, and 19.1 made free throws per game, with opponents held to 68.8 points and 39.2% shooting. That combination of paint scoring, glass control, and foul pressure is the backbone of Tommy Lloyd’s 2025-26 team. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/12/arizona-wildcats))

Offensively, Arizona plays through traditional advantages: early rim runs by Motiejus Krivas, deep seals and second-shot work from Tobe Awaka, and downhill guard play from Brayden Burries and Jaden Bradley. The numbers show the shape of the system. Arizona averages only 5.9 made threes per game in the official team stats despite shooting a respectable 36.0%, but it makes 19.1 free throws per game and dominates the interior with 434 offensive rebounds in 34 games. Against Houston on February 21, 2026, the Wildcats won 73-66 with a 38-20 edge in paint points and turned 16 turnovers into 16 points; that is classic Arizona this year: pressure the lane, punish mistakes, and trust size. Against Baylor on February 24, Arizona erased a 41-34 halftime deficit and won 87-80 by scoring 53 second-half points, outrebounding Baylor 37-30, and winning second-chance points 25-14. In practical scouting terms, Lloyd leans on horns-style entries into post touches, high ball screens for Bradley to create paint collapse, and wing isolation/post mismatch usage for Koa Peat and Burries. The evidence is in who finishes possessions: Burries leads the team with 542 points, Peat has 422 in only 31 games, Krivas has 356 on 58.2% shooting, and Awaka has 321 with 125 offensive rebounds. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The Wildcats’ preferred half-court pattern is to enter through Bradley, use Krivas as a screener or high-post hub, and crash relentlessly from the weak side with Awaka and Peat. Bradley’s 154 assists, 4.5 per game, make him the organizer; Krivas and Awaka are the interior finishers; Burries is the late-clock shot maker. A named example of their ball-movement offense came against BYU on February 18, when Bradley posted 12 points and a career-high-tying 10 assists in a 75-68 win, and Arizona’s bench added 26 points. Another came against Baylor, where Bradley had 25 points, six assists, and six rebounds, while Burries added 24 and Awaka posted a 10-point, 13-rebound double-double. Arizona does not rely on one action repeated mindlessly; it flows from ball screen to duck-in to offensive rebound, but the constant is this: Lloyd wants the possession to end at the rim, at the foul line, or with an inside-out three from a set defense already bent. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Defensively, Arizona is a traditional length-and-positioning team more than a gambling full-court unit. The official numbers are clear: opponents shoot 39.2% overall and 31.4% from three. Krivas protects the rim with 62 blocks, 1.8 per game; Awaka controls the glass at 9.5 rebounds per game; Burries, Bradley, and Ivan Kharchenkov are the point-of-attack disruptors with 54, 52, and 49 steals respectively. The defensive philosophy is to crowd the paint with size, contest without over-rotating, and finish the stop with a rebound. The best documented example came at Houston on February 21: Arizona held the Cougars without a field goal for nearly 10 minutes in the second half, forced a 12-0 run with tightened rotations, and limited Houston to 11-of-32 shooting after halftime. Another came in the 73-57 title-clinching win over Iowa State on March 2, when Arizona forced 16 turnovers and held the Cyclones to 29.2% shooting overall and 7-of-30 from three. This is not an overextended pressure defense; it is a disciplined shell with elite size behind the ball. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Tommy Lloyd’s coaching philosophy remains consistent with his Gonzaga roots but is more physical at Arizona: pace when available, spacing around skilled bigs, and trust in depth. Documented in-game adjustment history is a major tournament positive. Against Baylor on February 24, Arizona trailed by seven at halftime, then shot 54.5% after halftime and flipped the game with better shot selection and defensive stops. Against Houston on February 21, Lloyd’s team answered a 44-42 deficit early in the second half by tightening rotations, contesting nearly every look, and springing Dell’Orso off the bench for the go-ahead three that started the decisive run. Against Texas Tech on February 14, Arizona still showed a useful counter even in defeat: after trailing late, Ivan Kharchenkov’s late free throws forced overtime in a game with 11 ties and 11 lead changes, evidence that Lloyd’s late-game packages can still manufacture points under pressure even when the offense bogs down. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/news/2026/2/24/mens-basketball-arizona-takes-down-baylor-in-waco-87-80.aspx))

Clutch and late-game execution is mostly a strength, though not flawless. Arizona won at Houston, 73-66, on February 21 by finishing a 12-0 second-half run and then getting 14 of its final 23 points from Dell’Orso and Bradley. It won at Baylor, 87-80, on February 24 despite 14 lead changes and 10 ties, closing with 18-of-23 foul shooting. It also handled BYU, 75-68, on February 18 by extending a seven-point halftime lead to as many as 16 and never losing control in the final stretch. The warning tape is Texas Tech: Arizona lost 78-75 in overtime on February 14 after leading for more than 26 minutes; Tech’s 11 made threes and better overtime execution exposed Arizona’s one soft spot, which is that games can tighten if the opponent survives the first paint war and forces the Wildcats to match perimeter shot-making. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/news/2026/2/21/mens-basketball-no-4-arizonas-defense-stiffles-no-2-houston.aspx))

Key players start with Brayden Burries, the lead scorer at 15.9 points per game, plus 4.7 rebounds, 2.5 assists, and 1.6 steals. His recent form is excellent: 31 points, seven rebounds, and five steals at Colorado on March 7; 24 at Baylor on February 24; and 11 points with six rebounds against Iowa State on March 2. He also had a season-high 13 free throws made against BYU on January 26, a sign of his downhill pressure. Jaden Bradley is the engine guard: 13.3 points and 4.5 assists per game, with 154 total assists. His standout stretch included 25 points, six assists, and six rebounds at Baylor, plus 12 points and 10 assists against BYU. Tobe Awaka is the glass-and-force forward: 9.4 points and 9.5 rebounds, including 125 offensive boards; he had 13 rebounds and 10 points at Baylor, and 16 points with 12 rebounds against Texas Tech. Motiejus Krivas gives Arizona a true interior anchor at 10.5 points, 8.1 rebounds, and 1.8 blocks; he posted six blocks against both South Dakota State and Kansas. Koa Peat adds 13.6 points and 5.3 rebounds in 31 games and is the secondary mismatch forward, while Anthony Dell’Orso is the proven bench detonator, scoring 22 against BYU and another 22 at Houston on back-to-back nights. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/12/arizona-wildcats))

The notable wins tell you Arizona’s ceiling. The 96-75 win at Alabama on December 13, 2025 showed comeback power against a top opponent; Burries scored 28 as Arizona used a 14-1 second-half run. The 73-66 road win at No. 2 Houston on February 21 proved the Wildcats can win a rock fight away from home. The 84-61 win over No. 14 Kansas on February 28 and the 73-57 win over No. 6 Iowa State on March 2 showed championship poise, especially because Iowa State was held under 30% shooting. The losses are equally instructive. Texas Tech’s 78-75 overtime win on February 14 exposed Arizona’s vulnerability to shot-making variance and late-clock perimeter creation. The other loss matters less as a red flag because Arizona still closed the regular season 29-2 and then reached 32-2 by Selection Sunday, but any opponent with multiple pull-up shooters will study the Tech tape first. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/news/2025/12/13/mens-basketball-burries-scores-28-points-no-1-arizona-rallies-from-halftime-deficit-to-beat-no-12-alabama-96-75.aspx?utm_source=openai))

As for Lloyd’s NCAA tournament history, Arizona’s official bio says he has taken the Wildcats to the Sweet 16 in three of his first four seasons, including 2021-22, 2023-24, and 2024-25. The same Arizona bio lists his four-year record entering 2025-26 at 112-33, and notes that 2024-25 ended with another Sweet 16. His Gonzaga bio background also notes that as an assistant he was part of staffs that reached two national title games, two Elite Eights, and four Sweet 16s. For this specific Arizona job, the clear head-coach tournament résumé is: Sweet 16 in 2022, first-round exit in 2023, Sweet 16 in 2024, Sweet 16 in 2025. That track record, paired with a 32-2 Big 12 champion roster built on size, rebounding, and mature backcourt control, makes Arizona one of the safest high-seed profiles in the 2026 bracket. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/tommy-lloyd/5464?utm_source=openai))

Arizona enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with the profile of a true national-title contender, and the broadest consensus metrics all place Tommy Lloyd’s team in the top tier nationally. Through games of March 15, 2026, WarrenNolan lists Arizona at 32-2 with a NET rank of 3, BPI rank of 2, and KenPom/Pomeroy rank of 2. That alignment matters: this is not a team living on résumé inflation alone, nor one that is purely analytics-driven without elite wins. Arizona paired a No. 3 NET with top-two predictive metrics while also winning both the Big 12 regular-season and conference tournament titles and receiving a No. 1 seed in the West as the tournament’s second overall team. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

The clearest statistical takeaway is that Arizona is elite on both sides of the ball, but skewed slightly more toward offensive dominance than conventional “defense-first Arizona” stereotypes might suggest. One current KenPom-style roundup updated March 18 slots the Wildcats 11th nationally in adjusted offensive efficiency and 3rd in adjusted defensive efficiency, while another March tournament preview placed them 6th in AdjO and 12th in AdjD. Those exact placements differ by source, but the stable conclusion is strong: Arizona is operating as a top-10ish offense and top-15-or-better defense, with some systems viewing the defense as even more dominant. RotoWire’s team scouting page is more concrete on raw efficiency, listing Arizona at 1.27 points per possession on offense and 0.89 allowed on defense, rankings 7th and 2nd nationally respectively. Converting that to a per-100-possession frame yields roughly 127 offensive points and 89 defensive points per 100 possessions. ([cleatz.com](https://cleatz.com/latest-kenpom-rankings/))

Stylistically, Arizona is not a bombing team; it is a pressure-through-efficiency team. Axios noted that the Wildcats “attempt fewer three-pointers than almost any other team,” though they still make a respectable 36% from deep. Yahoo’s historical comparison piece quantified that shot mix more precisely, saying only 27.4% of Arizona’s shots came from three through the early undefeated stretch. That is a very low three-point attempt rate for a modern contender and fits the eye test: Arizona’s offense is built around rim pressure, post touches, offensive rebounding, transition flow, and free-throw generation more than perimeter volume. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/phoenix/2026/03/16/arizona-wildcats-no-1-seed-west-region-march-madness))

The available component stats reinforce that identity. RotoWire lists Arizona’s offensive turnover rate at 13.10%, good for 60th nationally, meaning this is a relatively secure offense but not an extreme low-turnover machine. On the glass and at the line, however, the Wildcats are much more forceful: their offensive FTA/FGA is 42.86, ranking 24th nationally, and their interior size has powered one of the country’s best two-point attacks. RotoWire describes Arizona as top-five nationally in both offensive and defensive two-point field-goal percentage, while Axios reports the Wildcats are the fourth-best rebounding team in the country. Big 12 game notes from Houston list Arizona at 13.23 offensive rebounds per game, 25th nationally as of February 19. Put together, the eFG story is clear even where exact national dashboard numbers are not freely accessible: Arizona creates efficient shots inside, converts them at a high rate, and supplements that with second chances and free throws rather than huge three-point volume. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/arizona-1291?utm_source=openai))

Pace is another important part of the profile. Arizona is not merely efficient; it plays fast enough to magnify that efficiency. Sports Illustrated’s Cincinnati preview identified the Wildcats as 25th nationally in tempo, and Yahoo compared this team to the 2013-14 Arizona group by noting Lloyd’s current team plays more than eight adjusted possessions per 40 minutes faster than that slower Sean Miller team. That suggests an adjusted pace in roughly the low-70s per 40 range, consistent with an up-tempo but still controlled contender rather than a frantic run-and-gun outfit. ([si.com](https://www.si.com/college/cincinnati/basketball/cincinnati-bearcats-basketball-2025-26-storylines-no-1-arizona-wildcats-01kfdnc512n9?utm_source=openai))

Schedule quality strengthens the case that the numbers are real. WarrenNolan’s current NET SOS page shows Arizona with the No. 4 strength of schedule nationally and a No. 34 non-conference SOS. Axios also reported in February that ESPN viewed Arizona as having the third-toughest remaining schedule at that point. In other words, these efficiency results were produced against a genuinely difficult slate, not padded by a soft league environment. That matters because Arizona’s raw record could otherwise tempt observers to dismiss some of the gaudier efficiency margins as a product of weaker opposition. The opposite is true: a 32-2 mark with a top-four SOS is about as sturdy a profile as exists in the field. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2025/sos-net?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is equally strong. Arizona closed the pre-tournament phase by winning the Big 12 tournament, including an 81-59 win over UCF and a 79-74 title-game win over Houston. RotoWire’s March 14 update also places Arizona fully healthy entering the tournament after Koa Peat’s late-February absence. The available “last 10” snapshot from a February Washington Post game preview had Arizona at 9-1 over its previous 10, averaging 86.0 points, 41.6 rebounds, 16.2 assists, 7.8 steals and 5.0 blocks while shooting 50.0% from the field. That aligns with the broader season picture: the Wildcats’ trend line is still that of a power team, not one limping into March. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/arizona-1291))

Where does the statistical profile diverge from conventional wisdom or the eye test? First, Arizona’s biggest perceived weakness is outside shooting, and that is directionally fair, but the more precise truth is that volume is the issue more than accuracy. They are not a bad three-point shooting team; they are a low-volume one, hitting around 36% while simply declining to build the offense around threes. Second, despite the old Arizona brand association with skill and pace, this team’s underlying dominance is probably more physical than many viewers assume. The rebounding, free-throw rate, interior scoring, and rim protection suggest a bruising frontcourt-driven machine disguised by Tommy Lloyd’s flowing tempo. Third, while casual observers may describe them as offense-led because of the scoring totals and undefeated start, predictive systems and possession-level data imply the defense may be just as bankable, and in some models even better. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/phoenix/2026/03/16/arizona-wildcats-no-1-seed-west-region-march-madness))

Overall, Arizona’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a balanced super-elite team with very few statistical holes. The Wildcats have top-three résumé metrics, top-two predictive rankings, elite per-possession scoring margin, a fast but not reckless pace, high-end rebounding, strong free-throw pressure, and enough shooting to keep defenses honest without depending on variance-heavy three-point barrages. If there is a subtle risk in the profile, it is that low three-point attempt rate can compress comeback paths or late-game shot-profile flexibility against equally elite opponents. But the broader data says Arizona is exactly what a No. 1 seed should be: physically imposing, analytically validated, battle-tested by schedule strength, and entering the bracket with championship-caliber form. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
Arizona is built to win with paint volume, offensive glass pressure, and foul pressure, not with high-volume perimeter shotmaking. Arizona is scoring 86.7 points per game, shooting 50.2% from the field, averaging 43.0 rebounds, 17.4 assists, and 19.4 made free throws per game, while only attempting 16.4 threes per game; just 26.5% of its field-goal attempts come from three, which Arizona’s own game notes say ranks 363rd out of 365 Division I teams on KenPom. The Wildcats also rank ninth nationally in fastbreak points at 17.0 per game. That profile tells you exactly what their offense wants: rim attacks from Jaden Bradley and Brayden Burries, duck-ins and seals for 7-foot-2 Motiejus Krivas, extra possessions from Tobe Awaka, and transition rim runs from their big frontcourt. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

The specific tactics that disrupt Arizona are the ones that flatten the paint and force jump-shot volume late in the clock. Because Arizona is so low-volume from three, the cleanest anti-Arizona script is to load the lane with a compact shell, stunt off weaker-volume shooters, and make the possession end with contested catch-and-shoot threes rather than paint touches or free throws. There are game examples. In Arizona’s 77-51 win over Cincinnati, the Wildcats won comfortably because their defense dominated, but offensively they still made only 3 of 13 threes. In the 84-77 win over UCF, they again took only 13 threes. In the 73-57 win over Iowa State on March 2, Arizona shot just 29.2% from the floor and 23.3% from three, a clear example of an opponent dragging them into a half-court grinder and cutting off efficient paint rhythm. BYU also did it in the Feb. 18, 2026 meeting, holding Arizona to 75 points on 43.1% shooting and only 5-of-19 from three. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

On press vulnerability, the available 2025-26 evidence suggests Arizona is not especially easy to rattle with pure pressure, but they can be bothered if the pressure is attached to pace control and physical rebounding denial. As a team they average only 11.0 turnovers per game with a 1.6 assist/turnover ratio, and Bradley individually has 125 assists against 45 turnovers. Against Houston on Feb. 21, one of the nation’s best pressure-and-physicality defenses, Arizona had only five turnovers and turned Houston’s 16 turnovers into 16 points. So blind pressing is not the answer. The better version is selective backcourt heat that burns clock, followed by a loaded lane in the half court. Houston’s loss is still instructive because Arizona solved the turnovers; teams trying to beat Arizona should note that simple pressure alone did not work. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

Zone vulnerability is more plausible than press vulnerability because Arizona’s shot diet is so anti-modern. When an opponent can sit in gaps and force them into above-the-break jumpers, Arizona’s efficiency dips. The statistical reason is straightforward: only 5.8 made threes per game, 35.3% from deep overall, and only 16.4 attempts per game. That means Arizona does not usually punish zone by sheer volume. The named-game evidence is BYU on Feb. 18, when Arizona scored only 75 and went 5-of-19 from three, and Iowa State on March 2, when Arizona managed only 57 points and shot 19-of-65 overall. Even in wins, low-volume perimeter outputs show the offense can get sticky if the paint is crowded. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

Arizona’s preferred pace is fast-but-controlled, roughly 70.1 possessions per 40 minutes by KenPom, with elite transition output layered on top of half-court physicality. Their own notes list them ninth nationally in fastbreak points, and they also rank sixth nationally in scoring margin. To force the opposite, you have to do three things together: send multiple defenders back on the shot, eliminate live-ball turnovers, and make Arizona guard for a full possession before attacking Krivas in ball-screen space. Iowa State’s 73-57 loss to Arizona still showed the general template for pace suppression because Arizona’s offense dropped to 57 points; BYU’s 75-68 win over Arizona on Feb. 18 is another example of a lower-scoring environment reducing Arizona’s edge. If the game stays in the high 60s or low 70s, Arizona’s talent advantage matters less because so much of its separation comes from transition bursts, offensive rebounding waves, and free-throw accumulation. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/index.php?error=1&utm_source=openai))

The size and athleticism issue is real at every spot. At point guard, Bradley is 13.5 points and 4.6 assists per game and gets downhill with strength; a small guard can be dislodged at the nail. At the two, Brayden Burries is a 6-foot-4, 205-pound freshman scoring 15.2 per game and had already logged eight 20-point games by late February. At the wing, Ivan Kharchenkov gives them a bigger forward body and secondary rebounding. At the four, Koa Peat is 6-foot-8, 235 and a power athlete who can overwhelm thinner combo forwards. At center, Krivas is 7-foot-2, 260 with 50 blocks, while Awaka adds a second bruising rebounder at 9.6 points and 9.4 rebounds. Arizona’s total rebounding margin is plus-11.6, with 43.0 rebounds per game to opponents’ 31.4. The practical mismatch map is this: 1) small guards get buried by Bradley’s paint pressure, 2) light wings get displaced by Burries and Kharchenkov, 3) finesse fours get punished by Peat and Awaka on the glass, and 4) single-coverage centers struggle with Krivas’ size. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/arizona.sidearmsports.com/documents/2026/2/23/28-_Arizona_Notes_-_at_Baylor.pdf))

Arizona leans more team offense than isolation-heavy offense, even though Bradley and Burries can bail possessions out. The best hard evidence available is structural rather than Synergy-coded: 17.4 assists per game, a 1.6 assist/turnover ratio, and multiple players in double figures. By late February, Arizona’s game notes listed 21 double-digit games for Burries, 20 for Koa Peat, 20 for Bradley, 18 for Kharchenkov, and 15 for Krivas. That balance says the offense is not one-star isolation dependent. Since no primary-source 2025-26 Synergy team page was publicly accessible in search, I cannot verify exact isolation-play percentages without risking invention; the safer evidence-based read is that Arizona is a shared-possession offense built around drives, interior touches, and second chances rather than a high-iso shot-creator model. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

Transition offense is clearly central; transition defense is also strong. Arizona averages 17.0 fastbreak points per game and allows just 68.6 points per game overall while holding opponents to 38.8% shooting. Against Alabama on Dec. 13, Arizona won 96-75 in a game with 52 rebounds and 20 assists, the type of up-tempo, chance-rich game they want. Against Kansas State on Jan. 7, Arizona scored 101 with 55 rebounds. Against Houston on Feb. 21, Arizona showed the defensive side of the transition battle by committing only five turnovers; that prevented Houston from getting easy runouts. So the defensive game plan against Arizona is not only “stop their break,” but “do not feed their break.” ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))

On coaching adaptability, the evidence is mixed. Tommy Lloyd’s teams clearly can make in-game pushes; for example, Arizona used a 16-0 second-half run to break open the Feb. 28 win over Kansas, and against Houston on Feb. 21 the Wildcats used a 12-0 second-half run while holding the Cougars scoreless from 14:16 to 7:16. Those are concrete examples of bench-to-bench adjustment windows producing separation. But there is also direct evidence of limits: after the Feb. 9 loss at Kansas, Lloyd said that when he learned Darryn Peterson would be out, Arizona made “not really” any adjustments. So the staff is strong at sustaining its own identity and finding second-half stretches, but not necessarily hyper-reactive to every opponent curveball. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/news/2026/2/28/mens-basketball-no-2-arizona-takes-down-no-14-kansas-at-home-84-61.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Arizona you must 1) play with two priorities on every shot attempt—one crash defender at most, four sprinting back; 2) pack the lane and dare their lowest-volume perimeter lineups to take 20-plus threes; 3) avoid live-ball turnovers, because Arizona scores 15.8 points off turnovers and thrives when Bradley and Burries attack a tilted floor; 4) gang rebound with your guards, because Arizona is plus-11.6 on the glass and can beat you even on poor shooting nights with second chances; 5) pull Krivas away from the rim in spread ball-screen actions, making the 7-foot-2 center defend change-of-direction space; and 6) make Bradley a scorer over length rather than a creator spraying the ball around. If Arizona gets 40-plus rebounds, 15-plus free throws made, and a low-turnover transition game, you are probably dead. If you hold them under 10 fastbreak points, keep the rebounding margin near even, and turn the night into a 65- to 68-possession half-court game where they need jumpers, you have a real upset path. ([arizonawildcats.com](https://arizonawildcats.com/cumestats.aspx?path=mbball))
